lead: A transducer converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, or an electrical signal into motion. A sensor measures; a solenoid acts. Aircraft use transducers for engine control, air data, fuel quantity, flight controls and health monitoring. The electrical form matters because it can be wired, multiplexed and checked. This chapter covers solenoids, pressure, temperature, strain, rotary position and acceleration, with the common signal forms and typical aircraft uses.
prereq: You need: basic electrical quantities and the signal-flow view from 4.2; the detailed conditioning circuits come in 4.11.

blocks.text: An aircraft cannot read pressure, heat or position directly. A transducer converts one physical quantity, the measurand, into an electrical signal; the reverse direction is actuation. A sensor is a transducer used for measurement. A solenoid is a transducer used for action. Active transducers generate a signal from the physical effect, such as a thermocouple. Passive transducers change resistance or capacitance and need excitation. Output may be voltage, current, resistance, frequency or a switch state. Avionics uses transducers in engine control, air data, fuel quantity, flight controls and health monitoring. Electrical output is easy to wire, multiplex and check. Signal conditioning and conversion follow in 4.11.

A solenoid is a coil with a movable iron plunger. Current in the coil creates a magnetic field and pulls the plunger against a spring. An on/off solenoid gives two states: energised or not. It opens a fuel shut-off valve or selects a hydraulic line. A proportional solenoid gives force roughly proportional to coil current; it trims a pressure valve. It is an actuator, not a measuring sensor.

Pressure is force per area, P = F/A, in pascal (Pa); 1 bar = 100000 Pa. A Bourdon tube is a curved flattened tube that straightens as pressure rises and moves a linkage. A diaphragm is a flexible disc that deflects under pressure. A strain-gauge pressure transducer bonds gauges to a diaphragm; pressure bends the diaphragm, the gauges stretch, and resistance changes. Absolute pressure uses a vacuum reference; gauge pressure uses local ambient. Aircraft use these for pitot-static air data, hydraulic pressure, fuel pressure and cabin pressure.
An RTD is a metal resistor, often platinum, whose resistance rises with temperature.

blocks.where: R<sub>T</sub> is resistance at temperature T in Ω; R<sub>0</sub> is resistance at T<sub>0</sub>; α is the temperature coefficient in 1/°C; T and T<sub>0</sub> are in °C.

blocks.text: It is stable and linear over a moderate range, but needs excitation current and can self-heat. A thermocouple joins two dissimilar metals. The hot junction produces a Seebeck emf proportional to the temperature difference between hot and cold junctions. It measures difference, not absolute temperature, unless cold-junction compensation is added. A thermistor is a semiconductor resistor with a large, nonlinear resistance change; it is sensitive but limited in range. Aircraft use thermocouples for exhaust gas temperature, RTDs for oil temperature and thermistors for cabin temperature.
A strain gauge is a thin conductor or foil bonded to a structure. When the structure stretches, the gauge lengthens and its resistance rises.

blocks.where: GF is gauge factor, dimensionless; ΔR is resistance change in Ω; R is unstrained resistance in Ω; ε = ΔL/L is strain, dimensionless.

blocks.text: A bridge circuit converts the small ΔR into a voltage. Strain gauges measure wing bending, landing-gear loads and pressure-diaphragm deflection.

A potentiometer uses a wiper on a resistive track. It gives a voltage divider output proportional to angle; simple, but the wiper wears. An LVDT has an AC-excited primary and two secondaries with a movable core. The secondary difference gives amplitude and phase proportional to displacement. An RVDT is the rotary form. A resolver has sine and cosine windings and gives robust angular information; aircraft use resolvers and RVDTs in flight-control and engine actuators.

An accelerometer has a proof mass. Acceleration moves the mass; piezoelectric material gives a charge, or a MEMS capacitor changes. Specify range in g, sensitivity in mV/g and number of axes. Aircraft use accelerometers in inertial systems, flight-data recording and stall or load monitoring. See Unit 5 for inertial navigation.

examples.question: A 350 Ω strain gauge has gauge factor 2 and is strained by 500 µε. Find the fractional resistance change and the change in resistance.
steps: Strain is given in microstrain: ε = 500 µε = 500 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.0005.
Use GF = (ΔR/R)/ε, so ΔR/R = GF × ε = 2 × 0.0005 = 0.001.
The fractional change is 0.001, which is 0.1 %.
examples.answer: The fractional resistance change is 0.001 and the resistance change is 0.35 Ω.
examples.check:
R = 350.0
GF = 2.0
eps = 500e-6
frac = GF * eps
dR = frac * R
print(f"{frac:.3f}")
print(f"{dR:.2f}")

traps: A solenoid is an actuator, not a sensor; a transducer can do both.
A thermocouple gives a temperature difference, not absolute temperature, without cold-junction compensation.
LVDT and RVDT outputs are AC and need demodulation; they are not simple DC potentiometers.
Pressure readings must state absolute or gauge; the wrong reference shifts every value.

quiz.q: Define transducer and sensor, and state the difference.
quiz.a: A transducer converts one physical quantity to an electrical signal, or the reverse. A sensor is a transducer used for measurement; an actuator such as a solenoid is a transducer used for action.

quiz.q: Why does a thermocouple need cold-junction compensation?
quiz.a: Its emf depends on the difference between hot and cold junction temperatures. To report absolute hot-junction temperature, the cold-junction temperature must be measured and added as compensation.

quiz.q: A platinum RTD has R₀ = 120 Ω at 20 °C and α = 0.00385 /°C. Find its resistance at 80 °C.
Compare a potentiometer and an LVDT for measuring flight-control surface position.
quiz.a: A potentiometer is simple and gives a DC voltage, but its wiper wears and it is less reliable. An LVDT has no sliding contact, is robust and gives an AC output proportional to displacement, but needs AC excitation and demodulation. For critical flight controls, the LVDT is preferred.

quiz.q: An accelerometer has sensitivity 100 mV/g. Its output is 0.45 V. Find the acceleration.
Why is a proportional solenoid used instead of an on/off solenoid in a pressure-control valve?
quiz.a: A proportional solenoid gives force that varies with coil current, so the valve can trim pressure smoothly. An on/off solenoid gives only fully open or fully closed states.

quiz.q: Why is a bridge circuit used with a strain gauge?
quiz.a: Strain changes gauge resistance by a very small amount. A bridge converts this small ΔR into a measurable voltage and can reject common-mode effects such as temperature changes when arranged correctly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern aircraft move toward smart digital transducers that linearise, compensate and test themselves, sending values on ARINC 429 or AFDX. MEMS accelerometers and pressure sensors dominate small UAVs because they are light and cheap. Research looks at fibre-optic strain sensing and wireless sensor nodes. Search for 'smart sensor', 'MEMS accelerometer aircraft', 'resolver-to-digital converter' and 'cold junction compensation'.
